strengths: Clear and well-motivated insight: The paper accurately identifies the discrepancy between T2I generation and image restoration, correctly pointing out that the conventional 4-channel latent space in Stable Diffusion causes irreversible high-frequency detail loss for SR, and justifies adopting a 16-channel VAE.

Methodological soundness: Adapting Score Identity Distillation (SiD) to conditional image restoration via Consistent Score Identity Distillation (CiD) and combining it with adversarial loss and representation alignment (CiDA) is well-formulated, addressing the score mismatch issue between noise generation and reconstruction.

Inference efficiency: The simplified inference pipeline removes the text encoder, tokenizer, and multi-step scheduler, allowing the one-step model to run in ~77ms with 933M parameters while preserving generative detail restoration capabilities.

Thorough evaluation: The method is validated across multiple synthetic and real-world benchmarks (ImageNet-Test, RealSR, RealSet80, RealLR200), demonstrating competitive or superior performance on perceptual and no-reference quality metrics (LIQE, MUSIQ, Q-Align), backed by human preference and MLLM (DepictQA) evaluations.
weaknesses: Perception-distortion trade-off: While GenDR excels in perceptual and no-reference quality metrics, its full-reference fidelity metrics (PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS in Table 2) are noticeably lower than both GAN baselines and some diffusion methods. A more nuanced analysis of potential hallucinations versus faithful detail recovery would strengthen the paper.

Base model training overhead: Retraining SD2.1 into SD2.1-VAE16 requires 100k iterations with a large batch size of 2048 on 8 A100 GPUs. The reliance on this newly trained base diffusion model makes reproduction non-trivial without releasing pre-trained checkpoints.

Prompt sensitivity and generalization: The pipeline completely fixes the prompt embeddings at inference time to remove the text encoder. While Table 5 shows comparable average MUSIQ scores, it remains unclear whether fixed prompts perform robustly across heavily semantic-dependent sub-domains (e.g., fine text, license plates, diverse face types) where conditioning typically helps guide restoration.
Minor typos and presentation errors: The manuscript contains minor typographical errors (e.g., 'demends' on page 2, 'visiual' on page 4, 'Implemetation' on page 5).

strengths: Clear problem motivation: The paper articulates the fundamental discrepancy between standard T2I diffusion models and real-world SR tasks, particularly identifying the 4-channel latent space compression and multi-step inversion as key bottlenecks for detail fidelity and inference speed.

Well-designed technical framework: Incorporating an open 16-channel VAE with SD2.1 via representation alignment (REPA) is an intuitive and effective solution to alleviate the detail-loss issue. Adapting score identity distillation (SiD) to SR by anchoring distillation to ground-truth targets (CiD/CiDA) with LoRA parameterization is methodologically sound.

Efficient deployment design: Streamlining the inference pipeline by eliminating the diffusion scheduler and pre-computing static text embeddings results in a highly efficient 1-step model (77ms per image), substantially outperforming multi-step methods in speed while remaining competitive with or exceeding existing one-step models.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The proposed method is evaluated across multiple standard synthetic and real-world benchmarks (ImageNet-Test, RealSR, RealSet80, RealLR200) using a wide suite of no-reference perceptual metrics, human evaluation, and DepictQA preference tests, accompanied by informative ablation studies.
weaknesses: Drop in objective fidelity / reconstruction metrics: GenDR exhibits noticeably lower PSNR and SSIM and higher (worse) LPIPS compared to GAN-based models (e.g., RealHATGAN) and several diffusion baselines on ImageNet-Test and RealSR. While generative detail restoration often trades distortion for perception, a deeper analysis or discussion regarding hallucination vs. structural fidelity would strengthen the paper.

Conceptual novelty is primarily an effective synthesis: The individual components (REPA, SiD, DMD2-style adversarial distillation, 16-channel VAEs) are largely existing techniques adapted and engineered together for the SR setting. While the system design is cohesive and effective, the theoretical novelty of the distillation formulation is somewhat incremental.

Training complexity and resource overhead: The overall training workflow requires pre-training SD2.1-VAE16, followed by multi-loss CiDA distillation (incorporating generator, two LoRA score networks, discriminator head, and DINOv2 feature extraction). More details regarding training stability, hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., balancing coefficients $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3$), and reproducibility would be beneficial.

Minor typographic and formatting issues: Minor typos exist in the text (e.g., 'demends' instead of 'demands' on page 2, missing spaces around symbols like 'GenDR *' throughout the draft, and formatting inconsistencies in Table 2).

strengths: Clear problem motivation: Identifying the trade-off between the 4-channel latent space constraint of standard text-to-image diffusion models and the detail preservation requirements of real-world super-resolution is insightful and well-articulated.

Well-engineered framework: Combining 16-channel latent representation alignment, an adapted Score Identity Distillation (CiD/CiDA), and pipeline simplification leads to a practical one-step restoration pipeline with impressive inference speed (77 ms per image).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The paper evaluates on both synthetic (ImageNet-Test) and real-world datasets (RealSR, RealSet80, RealLR200), reporting diverse no-reference and full-reference image quality metrics alongside user studies and MLLM-based evaluations (DepictQA).
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: The proposed framework largely combines existing techniques—such as REPA for representation alignment, Score Identity Distillation (SiD), DMD2-style adversarial objectives, and pre-trained 16-channel VAE weights—into an SR pipeline rather than introducing fundamentally new theoretical or methodological concepts.

Significant drop in fidelity/distortion metrics: While non-reference perceptual scores (LIQE, MUSIQ, Q-Align) are strong, distortion-based metrics (PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS) suffer notable drops compared to both GAN-based baselines and multi-step diffusion models (e.g., PSNR dropping below 24 dB on ImageNet-Test and RealSR). The paper lacks an in-depth analysis of the perception-distortion trade-off or failure modes caused by hallucinated artifacts.

Ablation studies could be more comprehensive: Key design choices, such as the fixed parameter setting for timesteps and diffusion schedules (setting $\bar{\alpha}_t = \bar{\beta}_t = 0.5$), the sensitivity to the loss balance hyperparameters $(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3)$, and the standalone impact of the 16-channel VAE without distillation, are insufficiently ablated quantitatively.

Writing and presentation issues: The manuscript contains multiple typographical and formatting errors (e.g., 'visiual', 'demends', 'Implemetation', 'Metics', and broken text layout in Section 4.1 / Figure references), which detracts from the overall presentation quality.

strengths: Insightful problem motivation: The paper identifies a fundamental mismatch between text-to-image (T2I) diffusion priors and real-world super-resolution (SR)—namely, that T2I benefits from a low-dimensional latent space (4-channel VAE) and multi-step sampling, whereas SR requires higher latent capacity (16-channel VAE) to preserve high-frequency details and can be executed in far fewer steps.

Well-designed technical framework: The authors construct a practical 0.9B SD2.1-VAE16 via representation alignment (REPA) rather than relying on prohibitively expensive DiT models (e.g., FLUX/SD3.5). Furthermore, the proposed Consistent Score Identity Distillation (CiD/CiDA) effectively resolves the training inconsistency between T2I distillation and SR targets by updating the real score network on HR images and replacing fluctuating generated latents with ground truth latents.

Impressive efficiency and practical deployment: By eliminating the diffusion scheduler and pre-computing prompt embeddings, the model runs in a single step with only 933M parameters and 77 ms latency on an A100 GPU. Practical deployment on server GPUs (A10, L20) using TensorRT demonstrates strong real-time throughput.

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: GenDR is thoroughly benchmarked against leading GAN-based and diffusion-based SR approaches across multiple synthetic and real-world datasets (RealSR, RealSet80, RealLR200). It establishes new state-of-the-art results among one-step diffusion models across modern perceptual quality metrics (e.g., Q-Align, MUSIQ, LIQE) and remains competitive with 50-step diffusion models.
Extensive ablations: The ablation studies systematically substantiate the benefits of the 16-channel VAE, the individual loss components of CiDA, CFG selection, and fixed-prompt strategies.
weaknesses: Perception-distortion trade-off and hallucination: While perceptual and no-reference quality metrics are markedly improved, full-reference metrics such as PSNR and SSIM show noticeable drops (e.g., 23.18 dB on RealSR compared to >26 dB for DiffBIR). While expected for generative SR, further analysis on structural hallucinations or fidelity boundaries would strengthen the paper.

Multi-stage training complexity: The complete training pipeline involves training SD2.1-VAE16, a two-stage generator warm-up (L1/perceptual loss), and finally CiDA distillation with multiple networks and LoRA heads. The end-to-end training procedure requires significant GPU compute and engineering effort.

Minor typographical and formatting errors: There are several minor presentation oversights in the manuscript (e.g., typo in Appendix title 'ALOGRORITHM DETAILS', formatting in Table headers, and slight notation clutter around Eq. 4-7).

strengths: Compelling and insightful motivation: The paper clearly identifies and analyzes the fundamental misalignment between T2I generation and image super-resolution, specifically highlighting how T2I benefits from compressed 4-channel latents whereas SR suffers severe irreversible high-frequency loss unless higher-capacity latents (16 channels) are utilized.

Well-designed and lightweight base model: Instead of relying on prohibitively heavy 16-channel DiT architectures (e.g., SD3.5 or FLUX), the authors successfully adapt SD2.1 to a 16-channel VAE space via representation alignment (SD2.1-VAE16), maintaining a modest 0.9B parameter budget while substantially improving detail preservation.

Principled step distillation formulation: The proposed Consistent Score Identity Distillation (CiD) addresses the distribution mismatch and instability of vanilla score distillation methods (VSD/SiD) when applied to restoration tasks by grounding the score networks on HR targets and applying an identity transformation. The extension to CiDA (with adversarial loss and REPA) further boosts perceptual sharpness.

High inference efficiency: The inference pipeline is streamlined by eliminating the noise scheduler, pruning the text encoder/tokenizer, and utilizing pre-computed fixed prompt embeddings, resulting in an impressive inference latency of 77ms on an A100 GPU.

Thorough and convincing empirical evaluation: GenDR demonstrates strong performance across standard benchmarks (ImageNet-Test, RealSR, RealSet80, RealLR200), convincingly outperforming existing one-step diffusion methods (SinSR, OSEDiff, InvSR) and matching or surpassing multi-step models (DiffBIR, DreamClear) across no-reference metrics, user studies, and MLLM evaluations.
weaknesses: Theoretical assumptions in CiD derivation: The mathematical justification in Appendix A.1 relies on the premise that the generator reaches the Bayes-optimal MSE minimizer $f_\theta^*(z_t, t) = \mathbb{E}[z_h | z_t]$. In practice, especially with adversarial and perceptual losses incorporated, the generator deviates from this conditional mean, which weakens the formal equivalence in Eq. (15).

Perception-distortion trade-off: While GenDR achieves top-tier scores in no-reference perceptual metrics (LIQE, MUSIQ, Q-Align), its full-reference metrics (PSNR/SSIM) are noticeably lower on several benchmarks compared to regression-oriented or even certain multi-step diffusion baselines. A more in-depth discussion on potential hallucinations versus fidelity to ground-truth structures would strengthen the analysis.

Training complexity: Although the inference pipeline is highly simplified and fast, the training framework (CiDA) requires optimizing and alternating between the generator, real score LoRA, fake score LoRA, and discriminator heads, which entails considerable GPU memory and engineering complexity (requiring 8x A100-80G GPUs).

Minor typographic and formatting errors: There are several minor typos throughout the paper (e.g., 'Alogrorithm Details' in Section A.2, 'Implemetation' in Section 3.3, and duplicated phrasing like 'apply Eq. (4) directly Eq. (4)' on page 5).

strengths: Insightful problem identification: The paper clearly identifies the fundamental mismatch in applying standard T2I diffusion models to real-world super-resolution (SR)—specifically, that standard 4-channel VAEs impose an irreversible information bottleneck on high-frequency details, whereas 16-channel diffusion transformer models (e.g., FLUX, SD3.5) are too computationally heavy for practical restoration tasks.

Tailored and practical base model: By adapting and training an SD2.1 model into a 16-channel VAE latent space (SD2.1-VAE16) via representation alignment (REPA), the authors preserve high reconstruction capability while maintaining an efficient model footprint (~0.9B parameters).

Novel SR-specific distillation strategy (CiD/CiDA): The proposed consistent score identity distillation modifies score distillation for paired restoration by using the target latent image in the identity transformation, stabilizing optimization and addressing distribution discrepancy. Integrating adversarial loss and representation alignment further boosts perceptual sharpness.

Streamlined inference and strong efficiency gains: The simplified pipeline removes the text encoder and diffusion scheduler during inference, achieving single-step inference in 77 ms (512x512 on A100) and outperforming existing one-step SR models across various non-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA) metrics and user/MLLM preference studies.

Extensive experimental validation: The paper provides thorough empirical comparisons across multiple benchmarks (ImageNet-Test, RealSR, RealSet80, RealLR200), detailed ablations of individual components (loss terms, latent channel capacity, prompt strategies), and practical deployment benchmarks (TensorRT on A10 and L20).
weaknesses: Perception-distortion trade-off: While GenDR excels in perceptual and non-reference quality metrics (e.g., MUSIQ, Q-Align, LIQE), its full-reference metrics (PSNR, SSIM, and occasionally LPIPS) drop noticeably compared to GAN-based and some multi-step diffusion baselines. A deeper discussion on the extent of generative hallucination versus faithful fidelity would strengthen the paper.

Incremental nature of core algorithmic components: The framework synthesizes several recently proposed concepts—REPA for latent alignment, SiD for score identity distillation, and DMD2-style adversarial objectives. While their combination and adaptation to paired SR are effective, the conceptual novelty of the individual distillation components is somewhat incremental.

Theoretical idealization in Appendix A.1: The derivation of CiD assumes the optimal MSE generator $f_\theta^*(z_t, t) = \mathbb{E}[z_h|z_t]$ holds throughout training. In practice, the generator is evolving and only approximates this conditional expectation, so the identity substitution introduces an approximation error that is not rigorously bounded.

Fixed prompt sensitivity: Although the simplified pipeline uses fixed prompt embeddings to bypass text encoding overhead, complex degradation cases (e.g., severe face degradation or fine text) may still benefit from input-dependent semantic cues, as shown in the ablation comparisons with VLMs.
